name: Git
description: The repository the panel is standing in, on one page: its branches, its log with the shape of the history drawn, what each commit touched and the difference itself.
author: xcommander

views.title: Git
views.description: The log of the repository this folder is in.

settings.label: Commits to read
settings.note: A log is walked from the tip, so this is how far back it goes. The status line says when it stopped short — a fork whose other side is one commit past the end looks exactly like no fork at all.

settings.label: Branches down the side as well
settings.note: The pill in the bar already says which branch you are on and opens the rest. This puts the whole list down the side too, which is a fifth of the window spent on something you glance at.

settings.label: Every branch, not only this one
settings.note: On, and it is what Fork shows. A log of one branch cannot draw a fork: the commit the branch left from is in it and the branch itself is not, so what was a fork comes out a straight line.

settings.label: Draw the shape of the history
settings.note: The lines down the left that say what came from where: a lane per line of development, a ring on a merge. With it on the log is ordered by its own shape rather than by date, because a parent has to be below its children for the lines to hold. Turn it off for a plain list, newest first.

settings.label: Show pictures of the people
settings.note: Off, and then nothing here touches the network. On, the application works out where a picture of each author might be from the address in the commit — GitHub for the addresses GitHub hands out, Gravatar for anybody else — and keeps what it finds on your disk. A row never waits for it: the ring shows initials until a picture arrives, and goes on showing them for anybody who has none.
